raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototype angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), combining neprilysin inhibition by sacubitrilat with angiotensin II type-1 receptor blockade by valsartan. Its rationale is biologically attractive in heart failure (HF): neprilysin inhibition augments natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and other vasoactive substrates, promoting natriuresis, vasodilation, cyclic guanosine monophosphate signaling, and antifibrotic effects, while concomitant renin–angiotensin system blockade prevents maladaptive angiotensin II accumulation [1,2]. The PARADIGM-HF program was designed to test whether this dual mechanism could improve outcomes beyond high-dose enalapril in ambulatory heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [3].

PARADIGM-HF established sacubitril/valsartan as disease-modifying therapy in chronic symptomatic HFrEF. In 8442 patients, sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or first HF hospitalization, as well as cardiovascular and all-cause mortality, compared with enalapril [4]. Subsequent analyses reinforced the clinical meaning of these findings: benefits extended to mode of death and to worsening-HF trajectories, including fewer emergency visits and need for treatment intensification [5,6]. Efficacy and safety were broadly consistent across age strata and systolic blood pressure categories, although hypotension was more frequent with ARNI and renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, and cough were generally less frequent than with enalapril [7,8]. Importantly, benefit persisted even when patients received lower-than-target doses, supporting initiation and titration rather than therapeutic nihilism in vulnerable patients [9]. Additional analyses suggested favorable metabolic and renal signals, including improved glycemic control in patients with diabetes and slower estimated glomerular filtration rate decline, albeit with modestly increased albuminuria in some settings [10,11]. Actuarial modeling projected clinically meaningful gains in survival and event-free survival, and population modeling suggested large potential public-health benefit if eligible HFrEF patients were treated [12,13].

The evidence base subsequently moved from stable ambulatory HFrEF to the vulnerable post-decompensation period. PIONEER-HF showed that, among hemodynamically stabilized patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HFrEF, in-hospital sacubitril/valsartan produced greater early NT-proBNP reduction than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, or angioedema [14]. Exploratory clinical outcomes and biomarker analyses supported early biological and clinical separation, including reductions in myocardial injury and wall-stress markers [15,16]. Open-label extension and dose-level analyses supported continued treatment after discharge and suggested that benefit was not confined to those rapidly achieving target dose [17,18]. TRANSITION complemented these data by showing feasibility of pre-discharge or early post-discharge initiation after stabilization [19]. Mechanistic outpatient studies further showed associations between NT-proBNP reduction and reverse cardiac remodeling, while EVALUATE-HF did not significantly improve its primary aortic stiffness endpoint but provided additional safety and structural data [20,21].

In HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), results have been more nuanced. PARAMOUNT demonstrated greater NT-proBNP reduction with LCZ696 than valsartan over 12 weeks, and a companion analysis suggested relative preservation of renal function [22,23]. However, PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death in patients with left ventricular ejection fraction ≥45%, although prespecified and exploratory analyses suggested greater benefit at lower ejection fractions and in women [24]. Renal analyses in PARAGON-HF showed less decline in kidney function with sacubitril/valsartan than valsartan [25]. Pooled analyses across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF support a continuum of benefit, greatest in HFrEF and attenuating as ejection fraction rises, with possible extension into HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) and “below-normal” preserved ejection fraction [26]. PARAGLIDE-HF and pooled PARAGLIDE-HF/PARAGON-HF analyses further suggest that after worsening HF with EF >40%, sacubitril/valsartan reduces NT-proBNP and may reduce worsening HF and renal events, at the cost of more symptomatic hypotension [27,28].

Current guidelines therefore position sacubitril/valsartan as foundational therapy for symptomatic chronic HFrEF, preferably replacing ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy when tolerated, and as a consideration in selected HFmrEF/HFpEF patients, particularly those with EF at the lower end of the preserved range [29,30]. Practical use requires attention to blood pressure, renal function, potassium, cost, and the mandatory 36-hour washout after ACE inhibitors to reduce angioedema risk. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan has shifted HF treatment from isolated neurohormonal blockade toward simultaneous suppression of maladaptive vasoconstrictor pathways and enhancement of endogenous compensatory peptide systems. Its strongest evidence remains HFrEF, but expanding trial data support individualized use across a broader EF spectrum, especially after worsening HF and in patients with EF below or near normal rather than truly preserved systolic function.
